# Abstract {.unnumbered .unlisted}

### English Version

No published study has yet demonstrated an automated pipeline for the binary morphological classification of mast cells in bone marrow aspirates aligned directly with a clinical diagnostic threshold. This thesis closes that gap. A YOLO11n object detection model was fine-tuned from a domain-specific pretrained checkpoint on annotated data from eight patients provided by the University Hospital Zurich, and evaluated under a leave-one-patient-out cross-validation scheme designed to reflect the real clinical question: can the model generalize to a patient it has never seen before? The training strategy was built on a series of empirical discoveries: that the default YOLO learning rate causes catastrophic forgetting when fine-tuning from a domain-adapted checkpoint; that disk-baked augmentation provides no regularization benefit beyond the first epoch; that the automated YOLO hyperparameter tuner converges on configurations that directly contradict the evidence from a systematic design-of-experiments sweep; and that standard augmentation techniques designed for natural-scene detection actively harm single-cell morphology classification. The resulting pipeline achieves a mean recall of 0.866 (R_Atypisch: 0.892, R_Normal: 0.840) and mAP50 of 0.864 across eight independent patient holdouts. A model-assisted annotation workflow using CVAT with NUCLIO integration bootstrapped an eight-patient labeled corpus from a single-patient starting point, establishing a self-reinforcing data flywheel that continues producing training data as the model is used clinically. A standalone PySide6 desktop application was developed and packaged as a self-contained Windows executable, solving the problem of running inference on up to 20,000 slide tiles per patient session through a chunk-based processing architecture. The trained weights have been delivered to the USZ for active deployment and prospective data collection.

{{< pagebreak >}}

### German Version

Bisher existiert keine publizierte Studie, die eine automatisierte Pipeline zur binären morphologischen Klassifikation von Mastzellen in Knochenmarkaspiraten beschreibt, die direkt auf ein klinisches Diagnosekriterium ausgerichtet ist. Diese Bachelorarbeit schliesst diese Lücke. Ein YOLO11n-Objekterkennungsmodell wurde ausgehend von einem domänenspezifisch vortrainierten Checkpoint auf annotierten Daten von acht Patienten des Universitätsspitals Zürich feinabgestimmt und mithilfe einer Leave-One-Patient-Out-Kreuzvalidierung bewertet, die die klinisch relevante Frage widerspiegelt: Kann das Modell auf einen Patienten generalisieren, den es noch nie gesehen hat? Die Trainingsstrategie basiert auf einer Reihe empirischer Erkenntnisse: dass die Standard-Lernrate von YOLO katastrophales Vergessen verursacht, wenn von einem domänenadaptierten Checkpoint weitertrainiert wird; dass vorab gespeicherte Augmentierungen nach der ersten Epoche keinen Regularisierungsvorteil mehr bieten; dass der automatische YOLO-Hyperparameter-Tuner auf Konfigurationen konvergiert, die dem systematischen Design-of-Experiments-Sweep direkt widersprechen; und dass Standardaugmentierungen für natürliche Szenenbilder die Klassifikation einzelliger Morphologie aktiv verschlechtern. Die resultierende Pipeline erzielt einen mittleren Recall von 0,866 (R_Atypisch: 0,892, R_Normal: 0,840) und einen mAP50 von 0,864 über acht unabhängige Patientenvalidierungen. Ein modellgestützter Annotationsworkflow auf Basis von CVAT mit NUCLIO-Integration ermöglichte den Aufbau eines acht Patienten umfassenden annotierten Datensatzes ausgehend von einem einzigen Patienten und etablierte einen sich selbst verstärkenden Datenzyklus, der mit der klinischen Nutzung des Modells weiter Trainingsdaten produziert. Eine eigenständige PySide6-Desktop-Applikation wurde als selbstenthaltendes Windows-Executable entwickelt, das das Problem der Verarbeitung von bis zu 20.000 Kacheln pro Patientensitzung durch eine chunk-basierte Verarbeitungsarchitektur löst. Die trainierten Gewichte wurden dem USZ zur aktiven Nutzung und prospektiven Datenerhebung übergeben.

# Methodology — Technical Sections
# (Replace the German placeholder text and all empty subsection headers)

## Technical

### General Data Information

The starting point for this project was a dataset of deliberately unusual characteristics: eight digitized bone marrow aspirate slides from patients referred to the University Hospital Zurich for suspected or confirmed systemic mastocytosis, spanning a clinical spectrum that ranged from purely atypical presentations to slides containing no atypical cells at all. Each slide was digitized by a whole-slide scanner and subdivided into 512-pixel JPEG tiles, yielding a labeled corpus of 1,103 images carrying 1,124 Atypisch and 78 Normal mast cell bounding box annotations. The raw Atypisch-to-Normal class ratio of approximately 14:1 is not a data collection artifact: it reflects the underlying biology of the patient cohort.

Patients P1 through P4 are systemic mastocytosis cases with predominantly or exclusively atypical mast cell presentations. P1 is the most extreme case: no normal mast cells were biologically present in that specimen, so all 428 labeled images received Atypisch annotations and no Normal-class label was produced. Patients P5 through P8 represent the opposite end of the spectrum. P5 contains three Atypisch cells against eighteen Normal cells, P6 and P8 carry exclusively Normal annotations, and P7 presents a roughly balanced distribution. This patient-level heterogeneity, summarized in @tbl-dataset, proved to be the most important single characteristic of the dataset: it shaped the evaluation protocol, the oversampling strategy, and the interpretation of the results at every stage of the project.

| Patient | Labeled Images | Atypisch | Normal |
|---------|---------------|----------|--------|
| P1 | 428 | 482 | 2 |
| P2 | 417 | 449 | 6 |
| P3 | 61 | 60 | 4 |
| P4 | 126 | 122 | 6 |
| P5 | 21 | 3 | 18 |
| P6 | 6 | 0 | 6 |
| P7 | 20 | 8 | 12 |
| P8 | 24 | 0 | 24 |
| **Total** | **1,103** | **1,124** | **78** |

: Per-patient annotation counts across the full eight-patient corpus {#tbl-dataset}

Beyond the labeled tiles, the dataset was expanded with two additional categories of negative examples that proved important for training robustness. The first was a collection of unannotated background tiles confirmed not to contain any mast cells, providing the model with explicit training signal for non-cell slide regions. The second was a curated set of confirmed false-positive cases: tiles where an early model version had produced detections that the clinical expert reviewed and rejected. Rather than discarding these failure cases, they were systematically incorporated into subsequent training rounds as hard negatives, directly targeting the model's most persistent misclassifications rather than relying solely on randomly sampled background tiles.

### Data Acquisition & Annotation

The annotation of a rare and morphologically nuanced cell type in a specialized tissue context is not simply a labeling task: it is a clinical knowledge transfer problem. Correctly identifying and classifying mast cells in bone marrow aspirate images requires domain expertise that cannot be acquired from standard image labeling guidelines. For this project, annotation was performed by Robin Kosche, Assistenzarzt at the Klinik für Medizinische Onkologie und Hämatologie at the USZ, whose direct clinical experience with systemic mastocytosis patients provided the ground-truth definition of what constitutes an atypical versus a normal mast cell in this specific tissue context. The tool used throughout was CVAT (Computer Vision Annotation Tool), an open-source web-based annotation platform supporting multi-class bounding-box labeling with integration hooks for model-assisted pre-annotation workflows.

What made the annotation of eight patients feasible within the scope of a bachelor thesis was a model-assisted bootstrap cycle introduced from the second patient onward. For P1, every tile was reviewed and labeled entirely by hand. Since P1 presented exclusively with atypical morphology, all annotations were of the Atypisch class. These 428 labeled images were used to train the first version of the detection model, DL_Modell_FV.pt. From P2 onward, this model was deployed as a NUCLIO serverless function integrated directly into the CVAT annotation interface. NUCLIO enables a deep learning model to be served as a backend that CVAT queries on demand, receiving bounding-box predictions as pre-filled draft annotations in the labeling view. When the annotator opened a new tile, the model's predictions appeared immediately as candidate boxes that could be confirmed with a single click, adjusted, or deleted if incorrect.

This setup transformed the economics of annotation in a way that is transferable beyond this specific task. A purely manual workflow scales linearly with the number of tiles: each image requires the annotator to scan the field and draw boxes from scratch. With model pre-annotation, the clinician's task shifts from drawing to reviewing: candidate cells are already localized, and cognitive effort is concentrated on the morphological judgment. More importantly, the corrections that the annotator made specifically targeted the model's errors and ambiguities, rather than being randomly distributed across the dataset. Each annotation session thus simultaneously built the labeled corpus and diagnosed the current model's failure modes, producing higher-quality training signal than any manually drawn annotation could provide. In cases where cell morphology was genuinely ambiguous, the annotator consulted colleagues to reach a consensus, though no formal inter-rater agreement protocol was applied across the full dataset.

False-positive detections confirmed as incorrect by the clinician during inference review sessions were compiled into an Excel-based tracking sheet maintained at the USZ and imported into subsequent training configurations as hard negatives, forming the FP-negative component of the dataset.

### Data Preprocessing

Before the final preprocessing strategy was established, a conceptually appealing but ultimately flawed approach was tested and rejected, yielding an important negative finding. The initial idea was to pre-apply image augmentation transforms offline before training began, writing augmented copies of each training image to disk using the Albumentations library, with horizontal flip, brightness and contrast jitter, and affine rotation. The approach appeared to offer a straightforward way to artificially expand the training set. Investigation revealed a fundamental flaw in this reasoning: augmentation only regularizes training when the model sees a different random transformation of each image in each epoch. When augmented copies are baked to disk before training starts, the model sees exactly the same fixed set of transformed images in every epoch. After the first epoch, the stochastic variability has been exhausted and training proceeds on what is effectively an unaugmented dataset. The offline augmentation approach was abandoned, and with it a clear finding was established: static data expansion cannot substitute for on-the-fly stochastic augmentation in epoch-based regularization.

The final preprocessing strategy used YOLO's built-in on-the-fly pipeline, in which each training image receives a freshly sampled random transformation at every epoch. Three settings were fixed through a combination of domain reasoning and experimental evidence. Mosaic augmentation was disabled entirely (mosaic=0.0). Mosaic is a YOLO-specific compositing technique that merges four randomly sampled images into a single training sample; it is highly effective for natural-scene detection where objects appear at various scales and spatial configurations. In 512-pixel single-cell tiles, mosaic compositing destroys the morphological context that defines the cell, splitting or partially obscuring the features the model must classify. Applying mosaic to this task is equivalent to showing a pathologist four overlapping, truncated cell fragments and asking for a morphology judgment: the task becomes structurally impossible. Vertical flip was enabled at probability 0.5 (flipud=0.5), which is biologically valid because bone marrow cells have no canonical up-down orientation. Rotation of up to 5 degrees (degrees=5) was applied to introduce modest in-plane orientation variance. The value of 5 degrees was not chosen arbitrarily: it emerged as the winner of the systematic hyperparameter sweep described in the training section, with smaller values providing insufficient diversity and larger values measurably degrading Normal-class recall.

Addressing the 14:1 class imbalance required more than augmentation alone. A per-patient image oversampling strategy was designed for the LOPO training folds: the complete image sets of Normal-rich patients were duplicated multiple times via symbolic links, with multipliers calibrated to each patient's annotation density. P5's set was duplicated eightfold, P6's fifteenfold (given only six labeled images), P7's eightfold, and P8's tenfold. Combined with per-epoch on-the-fly augmentation, this brought the effective Atypisch-to-Normal ratio within each training fold to approximately 2:1, without fixing any additional augmented copies to disk and maintaining the full stochastic diversity of the on-the-fly pipeline.

### Model Selection & Architecture

The selection of YOLO11n (nano) as the detection backbone was reached through both theoretical reasoning and direct empirical comparison, not adopted as a default. YOLO11 is the eleventh generation of the You Only Look Once family of single-stage object detectors, which perform bounding-box localization and class prediction simultaneously in a single forward pass. The nano variant, with approximately 2.6 million parameters, represents the architecture's smallest footprint: fast enough for real-time inference on standard clinical workstation hardware and compact enough to avoid overfitting on the approximately 1,100-image corpus available for this project. A direct comparative test with YOLO11l, the large variant at more than twenty times the parameter count, confirmed that the additional capacity degraded rather than improved generalization. The larger model overfitted to training-set patterns that did not transfer across folds, producing worse test-set metrics than the nano variant on the same data. For rare-cell medical imaging datasets where annotation is the bottleneck and model capacity should match data size, the nano architecture is the appropriate choice, and the YOLO11l comparison validates this decision empirically rather than by assumption.

The model was configured for two-class detection: Atypisch (class 0) and Normal (class 1), the two morphological phenotypes whose ratio determines the WHO minor diagnostic criterion.

A critical architectural complication arose from the multi-phase training strategy. The domain-specific pretrained model used as the fine-tuning starting point for Phase 2, DL_Modell_FV.pt, had been trained originally with a single-class head (nc=1). Reloading it for two-class fine-tuning (nc=2) causes Ultralytics to internally rebuild the detection head's classification branch from random initialization, because the final convolutional layer's output dimension changes from 1 to 2 channels and the stored weights for that layer have incompatible shape. The bounding-box regression branch and all backbone layers transfer correctly, carrying domain-adapted feature representations forward. But the classification head, which must now distinguish Atypisch from Normal rather than simply detecting Atypisch, starts entirely from random weights. This means that at the beginning of every Phase 2 fine-tuning run, the network is in a structurally mixed state: the backbone extracts domain-relevant features, and the head predicts classes randomly. This combination has a specific and damaging failure mode that the project had to discover, characterize, and resolve before Phase 2 could produce meaningful results.

### Model Training & Fine-Tuning Strategy

Training proceeded in three phases, each building directly on findings made in the previous one rather than following a pre-set plan. The overall arc is as much a record of what was discovered as it is a record of what was built.

**Phase 1: Single-Patient Baseline (P1).** The first training phase was designed to establish what a modern YOLO architecture could achieve on the available data with no domain-specific starting point. Training used yolo11n.pt, the generic COCO-pretrained weights, applied to the P1 dataset with five-fold stratified cross-validation, patience-based early stopping (patience=50, up to 5,000 epochs), and cosine learning rate annealing. The result was revealing: validation mAP50 reached 0.952 in the best fold, confirming that the model could fit the P1 data distribution effectively, but the cross-fold mean was only 0.800 with a standard deviation of 0.129. Fold 5 collapsed at epoch 29 with a recall of 0.432: a single unlucky data split had placed the model in a local optimum from which it could not recover given the patience limit. The conclusion drawn from Phase 1 was not that the architecture was insufficient, but that generic COCO pretraining produced a training trajectory fragile enough that fold assignment determined outcome. A domain-specific starting point, one that had already adapted its feature representations to bone marrow cell morphology, was needed to produce a stable and reproducible training process.

**Phase 2: P2 Dataset Fine-Tuning Experiments.** Phase 2 set out to answer the question of how to correctly fine-tune from a domain-adapted checkpoint. The starting model, DL_Modell_FV.pt, is the model trained in Phase 1 on P1 data, repurposed as the fine-tuning base for the two-class problem on P2 data. Seven configurations were tested across variations of base model, learning rate, backbone freeze depth, and hyperparameter source.

The central discovery of Phase 2 was a learning rate mismatch that explains a failure mode easy to encounter but largely undocumented in YOLO deployment guides. At the default learning rate (lr0=0.01), the randomly initialized classification head produced large error gradients in early training epochs that propagated backward into the pretrained backbone and progressively overwrote its domain-adapted feature representations. The model converged, but to a high-precision, low-recall solution: it became overly conservative, detecting only the most obvious cells and ignoring borderline cases, because noisy early gradients had penalized ambiguous predictions before the backbone could stabilize. The result was P2-C: a domain-specific pretrained model with the default learning rate achieved recall of only 0.397, worse than training from generic COCO weights entirely. Reducing the learning rate to 0.001 and freezing the first ten backbone layers (freeze=10) resolved this. The pretrained feature extractor was held fixed while only the detection head adapted, allowing the head to converge on a meaningful classification signal before the backbone received any gradient updates. This recipe, applied to DL_Modell_FV.pt in run P2-D, recovered the domain pretraining advantage: test-set recall reached 0.655 and mAP50 reached 0.590.

A trial run using the YOLO built-in hyperparameter tuner (model.tune()) as the configuration source produced the most dramatic failure of the project. Classification loss exceeded 5.8 across all five folds in early training epochs, against a normal range of 0.5 to 1.5, and near-zero cross-fold variance (std=0.007) confirmed that all folds collapsed to the same degenerate solution. This is the signature of catastrophic forgetting: the tuner-recommended configuration, designed for from-scratch training, specified learning rate and regularization settings that caused the classification head's gradients to completely overwrite the backbone's pretrained representations within the first epochs. The model lost all benefit of domain pretraining. This result was preserved as a methodological negative finding with a clear practical implication: hyperparameter configurations generated by automated tuners for from-scratch training are not transfer-safe and will actively harm fine-tuning from domain-adapted weights.

**Phase 3: Full Eight-Patient Corpus, Leave-One-Patient-Out CV.** With the fine-tuning recipe confirmed, Phase 3 introduced two interconnected advances: expansion to the full eight-patient corpus and a fundamental change in the evaluation protocol. The shift from stratified k-fold to leave-one-patient-out (LOPO) cross-validation was a deliberate response to a data leakage problem that is easy to overlook and has serious consequences for reported metrics. Stratified k-fold distributes individual images across folds without regard for patient identity, which allows tiles from the same patient's slide to appear in both training and test. Within a single patient's data, staining intensity, scanner calibration, slide preparation technique, and cellular density are internally consistent, yet these properties vary substantially across patients. A model evaluated with k-fold can exploit this within-patient consistency to achieve inflated metrics that do not reflect genuine cross-patient generalization. LOPO eliminates this completely by ensuring that the held-out test patient is absent from training at every level. The performance figures reported in this thesis are therefore conservative estimates of true clinical generalization, not optimistic within-patient interpolations. For a tool intended to be applied to new patients arriving at a hospital, this is the only evaluation that answers the operationally relevant question.

A four-factor design-of-experiments matrix was run across all eight LOPO folds, varying label smoothing (0.0 vs. 0.1), rotation augmentation (0, 5, and 10 degrees), DFL loss weight (1.5 vs. 2.0), and backbone freeze depth (0 vs. 10 layers). Fourteen of the planned twenty-four configurations were completed before HPC queue limits were reached. Three findings emerged. First, label smoothing was confirmed as a complete no-op: configurations at ls=0.0 and ls=0.1 with identical other parameters produced bit-identical fold metrics, indicating that the parameter either does not reach the detection head's loss path in this Ultralytics version or is otherwise inert. Given this finding, the remaining unrun cells (all label_smoothing=0.1 variants) were not necessary to identify the winning configuration. Second, rotation at 5 degrees consistently outperformed both 0 and 10 degrees across all other parameter settings, with 10-degree rotation degrading Normal-class recall most noticeably, confirming the domain reasoning that large rotations are counterproductive for single-cell morphology classification. Third, a DFL loss weight of 1.5 consistently outperformed 2.0 on Normal-class recall across all tested freeze and rotation combinations. The winning configuration was degrees=5, dfl=1.5, freeze=10, label_smoothing=0.0.

The automated YOLO tuner was re-evaluated in Phase 3 under production-matching conditions. After 30 optimization iterations on a single-patient fold, it converged on degrees=0.0 and dfl=2.47, both of which directly contradict the matrix evidence: degrees=5 outperformed degrees=0 by approximately 4 percentage points on Normal recall, and higher DFL values consistently reduced Normal recall in the matrix. A full eight-fold LOPO validation of the tuner's output was therefore not carried out; the matrix evidence already predicted the outcome. This result strengthens the Phase 2 finding: the automated tuner and the systematic DoE matrix answer fundamentally different questions. The tuner maximizes a fitness score on a single patient fold, which is sensitive to that patient's specific characteristics and insensitive to what generalizes across the population. The DoE matrix, evaluated on all eight patients simultaneously, selects configurations that are robust to individual-patient heterogeneity. For a rare-class clinical application where per-class recall must hold across a heterogeneous patient cohort, systematic multi-patient evaluation is not optional.

All training was executed on ZHAW's HPC cluster (earth-4 partition, two NVIDIA L40S GPUs with 48 GB VRAM each) via SLURM job submission. Two infrastructure-level bugs were identified and corrected during the project. The first involved concurrent SLURM jobs sharing temporary workspace directories, causing cross-fold data collisions when multiple jobs ran simultaneously. This was fixed by namespacing all temporary paths with the SLURM_JOB_ID environment variable. The second involved the background-image sampling logic: the BG_RATIO parameter was evaluated correctly in the main process but the resulting image list was never forwarded to the per-fold training worker processes, meaning the parameter had no effect in several early Phase 2 experiments. This bug was identified and corrected before any Phase 3 runs were submitted.

The final deployment model was trained on all eight patients without a holdout, using the Phase 3 winning recipe. This follows standard post-cross-validation practice: the LOPO protocol produces the unbiased generalization estimate, and the final production model then exploits all available labeled data. The resulting best.pt weights file is the artifact delivered to the USZ.

### Model Testing

Ensuring that reported metrics are not contaminated by any information the model encountered during training required deliberate design of the test protocol at each phase. In Phase 1 and Phase 2, a strict three-way split was applied within each fold: separate training, validation, and test subsets, with the test subset excluded from every step of model fitting and early stopping. Validation metrics were used only to trigger patience-based stopping, never to compare configurations against each other. All between-run comparison was performed exclusively on test-set numbers. This design prevents a common evaluation pitfall: selecting among configurations based on validation performance effectively incorporates the validation set into model selection, which systematically inflates the apparent performance of the selected model.

In Phase 3 LOPO evaluation, each held-out patient constituted the test set for its fold by construction. Inference was run on each fold's best.pt checkpoint at a confidence threshold of 0.58 and an IoU threshold of 0.45. These thresholds were selected by analyzing the confidence distribution of predictions on held-out data and identifying the operating point that best serves the clinical priority for high recall, accepting a modest reduction in precision in exchange for minimizing missed cells. The eight-fold LOPO test-set means are the primary reported performance figures of this thesis, and fold-level deviations from those means reflect genuine biological and morphological heterogeneity between patients rather than statistical noise.

### Evaluation Metrics

The choice of metrics was determined by the clinical context before any model training began, establishing an evaluation priority that the training strategy then had to serve. The standard benchmark metric is mean Average Precision at IoU threshold 0.50 (mAP50), enabling comparison with published detection results on related tasks. mAP50-95, integrated across IoU thresholds from 0.50 to 0.95, provides a stricter localization measure that penalizes bounding boxes that correctly identify a cell but imprecisely locate its boundary.

Within the clinical context of this project, neither mAP metric is the primary decision criterion. Recall is. A missed mast cell is a false negative that silently removes a cell from the Atypisch fraction computation. If the missing cell was atypical, the fraction is understated; if it was normal, the fraction is overstated. Either way, the ratio shifts in a way that the clinician cannot easily detect, because missed cells leave no trace in the output. A false positive, by contrast, introduces a visible spurious detection that the clinician can identify and remove through the annotation editor during post-inference review. This asymmetry, that false negatives are invisible and false positives are correctable, makes recall the metric most closely aligned with clinical safety and drives every model selection decision throughout the project.

Per-class recall for Atypisch (R_Atypisch) and Normal (R_Normal) was tracked separately in all Phase 3 evaluations. The 14:1 class imbalance means that aggregate recall can appear satisfactory even when Normal-class detection is failing, because the majority class dominates the mean. Since correctly identifying Normal cells is required to compute a meaningful and unbiased Atypisch fraction, R_Normal is treated as the most clinically sensitive individual metric and the primary signal for selecting among configurations in the DoE matrix.

### UI Creation

Making the pipeline accessible to clinical users without a programming background required building a complete standalone graphical interface, and the path to the final application was defined by a failure that exposed a real constraint no prior tool in this area had addressed. An initial prototype was built as a Gradio web application. Gradio is a widely used rapid-prototyping framework for deploying models as browser-based tools, and the prototype was functionally complete for small-batch inference. The clinical workflow at the USZ, however, operates on image sets of approximately 20,000 tiles per patient session: the full digitized slide subdivided into overlapping 512-pixel tiles covering the entire specimen. No available hardware configuration could load a dataset of this size into a web server's memory in a single pass without crashing. The Gradio prototype was abandoned not because of a design flaw but because it surfaced a fundamental architectural constraint: clinical-scale bone marrow slide inference requires a processing strategy that does not assume the full dataset fits in memory at once, and a web-based architecture built around request-response semantics cannot satisfy this constraint without substantial reengineering.

The solution was a chunk-based processing architecture implemented in a standalone PySide6 desktop application named MastCellDetector. PySide6 provides official Qt for Python bindings, enabling a native-looking windowed interface with full hardware access. The application was compiled into a self-contained Windows executable using PyInstaller, bundling all Python dependencies into a single distributable folder that runs on a clinical workstation without requiring any Python installation or environment configuration. The inference pipeline divides the full image set into consecutive chunks of configurable size (default: 250 images per YOLO predict() call), processes each chunk and writes its results to disk before the next chunk is loaded, keeping peak memory usage bounded regardless of total dataset size. Inference runs in a dedicated QThread worker, keeping the interface fully responsive throughout processing and supporting user-initiated cancellation at any point.

The application was designed around the clinician's actual review workflow rather than around generic machine learning tool conventions. Three views cover the complete post-inference workflow. The gallery view presents all images as thumbnail tiles with detection metadata overlaid, supporting seven filter modes that allow the clinician to focus on the most relevant subsets: all images, images with detections, images without detections, low-confidence borderline cases, Atypisch-containing, Normal-containing, and manually edited images. The annotation editor provides full-resolution inspection of any tile with the model's predicted bounding boxes overlaid, and allows the clinician to add, delete, or reclassify individual boxes manually, with all corrections persisted across sessions via a JSON sidecar file alongside each image. The statistics view delivers the diagnostic-level output: the computed Atypisch fraction relative to the WHO 25% threshold, per-image cell count breakdowns, and the confidence score distribution across all detections, providing immediate at-a-glance context for whether the patient sample is above or below the diagnostic boundary. Additional features include automatic GPU detection with recommended batch size reporting, configurable confidence and IoU thresholds, integrated Google Drive folder download, and persistent settings across sessions.

The application was tested on real USZ patient data and operated correctly under clinical conditions. It was delivered to the clinical partner as the primary operational interface for the deployed model.

[Figure placeholder: Screenshots of the MastCellDetector desktop application showing (left) the gallery view with filter chips and detection thumbnails, (center) the annotation editor at full resolution with bounding box overlay, and (right) the statistics view with the Atypisch fraction bar relative to the WHO 25% threshold]

### Implementation in USZ Infrastructure

Integration of the pipeline into Cinderella, the proprietary cell classification software deployed at the USZ, was evaluated as a potential delivery pathway at the project's outset. This route was ultimately not pursued. The engineering work required to interface with Cinderella's internal API, combined with the IT governance and approval processes that govern software integration within a hospital IT environment, exceeded what could be accomplished within the thesis timeline. Rather than treating the standalone application as a fallback, it should be understood as a deliberate and justified delivery format: MastCellDetector is a self-contained, independently testable artifact that does not depend on any hospital software infrastructure, can be updated and redeployed without an IT approval cycle, and was fully tested with real patient data before handover. The trained model weights have been delivered to the USZ for active use within the existing clinical workflow and for inference on new patient slides as they become available. The experience accumulated through standalone deployment provides a concrete operational foundation for any future integration specification should the Cinderella pathway be revisited.

# Results

## Model Results and Statistical Evaluation

The three-phase development arc produced a progression of results that are best understood as a sequence of discoveries, each of which required a methodological response rather than a simple increment toward higher numbers. Phase 1 established that the task was feasible but that generic pretraining produced an unstable training process. Phase 2 revealed what fine-tuning from a domain-adapted checkpoint actually requires, at the cost of encountering and documenting two distinct failure modes. Phase 3 delivered the first clinically honest cross-patient performance estimate and established the final deployment configuration.

**Phase 1: P1 Dataset (yolo11n.pt, 5-fold CV)**

Training on P1 with generic COCO-pretrained weights showed that mAP50 ranged from 0.621 to 0.952 across five folds, with fold 5 terminating abnormally at epoch 29 due to early stopping. This outlier fold is not a sign of model weakness but of data split fragility: with only 428 labeled images from a single patient, a single unlucky fold assignment can place the validation set in an unrepresentative region of the image space. The mean mAP50 of 0.800 with standard deviation 0.129 confirmed feasibility but also confirmed that single-patient generic-pretrained training could not produce the consistency needed for a reliable pipeline.

| Fold | Best Epoch | mAP50 | mAP50-95 | Precision | Recall |
|------|-----------|-------|----------|-----------|--------|
| 1 | 135 | 0.952 | 0.805 | 0.884 | 0.920 |
| 2 | 112 | 0.756 | 0.583 | 0.634 | 0.780 |
| 3 | 120 | 0.893 | 0.745 | 0.764 | 0.737 |
| 4 | 128 | 0.775 | 0.637 | 0.671 | 0.725 |
| 5 | 29 | 0.621 | 0.473 | 0.887 | 0.432 |

**Phase 2: P2 Dataset Fine-Tuning Summary**

Phase 2 was a controlled experiment designed to discover the correct fine-tuning recipe, and the results table tells a story with two clear plot points: the failure of the default learning rate (P2-C) and the catastrophic failure of the automated tuner (P2-E).

: Phase 2 test-set results summary across all configurations {#tbl-phase2}

P2-C demonstrates the learning rate mismatch concretely: the domain-specific pretrained model at the default learning rate (0.01) produced recall of 0.397, 22 percentage points below the generic COCO baseline. P2-E demonstrates catastrophic forgetting: near-zero variance (std=0.007) means all five folds collapsed to the same degenerate solution. P2-D, using the discovered recipe of lr0=0.001 and freeze=10, recovered both performance and cross-fold variance to levels consistent with genuine learning.

The most meaningful improvement in the winning configuration is the R_Normal gain: from 0.754 in the Phase 3-A baseline to 0.840, an 8.6-percentage-point advance on the rarest and most diagnostically sensitive class. The winning configuration achieved a mean recall of **0.866** (R_Atypisch: 0.892, R_Normal: 0.840, mAP50: 0.864, mAP50-95: 0.741, Precision: 0.812) across all eight independent patient holdouts.

## Quantitative and Qualitative Evaluation

**Quantitative interpretation.** The headline recall of 0.866 means the deployed pipeline detects approximately 87 in every 100 mast cells present in a slide. Whether this is clinically sufficient depends on a property of the detection error that the per-class breakdown reveals: both classes are missed at similar rates. The 5.2-percentage-point gap between R_Atypisch and R_Normal in the winning configuration means the model's undercount is nearly proportional: if the true Atypisch fraction is 40%, the model's computed fraction approximates 40% rather than being systematically biased toward or away from the 25% diagnostic boundary. A detection system that missed Normal cells disproportionately would overstate the Atypisch fraction; one that missed Atypisch disproportionately would understate it. The near-proportional miss rate is therefore a clinically important property, and it was not present in the baseline: the Phase 3-A baseline showed a 10.8-percentage-point R_Atypisch to R_Normal gap (0.862 vs. 0.754), more than twice the winner's 5.2-point gap. The DoE sweep measurably improved class balance, not just aggregate performance.

A mean mAP50 of 0.864 places the pipeline within the range achieved by YOLO-family detectors on other hematological cell types in the published literature (approximately 77 to 94%), while operating on a corpus orders of magnitude smaller than those studies. This comparison suggests the current results are a floor, not a ceiling: they reflect the constraint of an eight-patient dataset, and expanding the corpus is the most direct path to further improvement.

**Qualitative interpretation.** The per-fold distribution in @tbl-lopo-baseline reveals the structure of the remaining performance gap. Folds 7 (P7 holdout, recall 1.000) and 8 (P8 holdout, recall 0.911) represent the strongest cases; folds 1 (P1 holdout, recall 0.626) and 5 (P5 holdout, recall 0.617) represent the weakest. These outlier folds are not random variation. P1 is the only patient in the corpus with no Normal-class labels, making it the only test case for which the training set provides no cross-patient Normal-cell signal from any other patient sharing that distributional context. P5 is the only Normal-dominated case in the dataset: three Atypisch against eighteen Normal cells, a prior distribution that no other training patient resembles. For both, the weaker performance reflects a genuine distributional mismatch between what the model was trained on and what it was tested on. These are not model failures: they are diagnostics of what is missing from the current training corpus.

[Figure placeholder: Per-fold recall bar chart for the winning configuration, with grouped bars for R_Atypisch and R_Normal per patient holdout]

## Evaluation Visualization

The per-fold recall plot makes visible what the means compress: the model performs consistently well across six of eight patients and degrades specifically on the two cases where the training distribution does not cover the test distribution. This pattern carries a predictive implication for clinical use. Cases that resemble the typical SM presentations of P2 through P4 and the Normal-rich patients P6 through P8 can be expected to produce recall in the range of 0.826 to 1.000. Cases resembling P1, purely atypical presentations, or P5, unusually Normal-dominated ones, should be flagged for more thorough manual review. The confidence score distribution across all predictions shows a polarized picture: the large majority of detections cluster at high confidence (above 0.85), with a small tail of borderline cases near the threshold. The annotation editor in the desktop application is specifically designed to make this borderline tail reviewable, focusing the clinician's limited review time where the model is least certain.

[Figure placeholder: Confidence score distribution histogram across all predictions, at conf=0.25 inference threshold, for the final deployment model]

[Figure placeholder: Side-by-side mAP50 comparison across all eight LOPO holdout patients, Phase 3-A baseline vs. winning configuration]

## Real World Usage

### Tests With Unseen Data

The desktop application was tested on real bone marrow aspirate slide data from the USZ that was not part of the training corpus. The model processed the full image set through the chunk-based inference pipeline without memory issues, producing per-image detection results and a patient-level statistics summary at a speed practical for clinical review. The statistics view correctly computed the Atypisch fraction from the aggregated detections and displayed it relative to the WHO 25% threshold, delivering the intended decision-support output under real clinical conditions rather than controlled test conditions.

Qualitative inspection of the output confirmed correct localization in the large majority of reviewed images. False negatives were concentrated on cells near tile boundaries, where partial visibility reduces the discriminative signal available to the detector: a limitation that tile overlap strategies could address in future iterations. False positives were sparse but present, consistent with the precision-recall tradeoff at the confidence threshold of 0.25 used in the review-mode interface. Critically, the clinician's ability to manually correct predictions through the annotation editor was verified during the session: corrections were persisted across sessions and excluded from re-inference, establishing an iterative review workflow where the quality of the output improves as the clinician works through the dataset.

The tested data is prospectively tracked for contribution to future training rounds. Each clinical session thus generates not only a diagnostic output but also labeled training data for the next model version, sustaining the self-reinforcing annotation loop that made the current eight-patient corpus possible.

[Figure placeholder: Example output tile from unseen USZ data, with bounding box overlays colored by class (Atypisch and Normal), at the deployed confidence threshold]

# Discussion

## Interpretation of Results

The progression from Phase 1 through Phase 3 is not a smooth curve of improvement. It is a sequence of findings, each of which changed how the next experiment was designed. That structure is itself a result worth discussing, because it reveals something about the challenge of applying modern deep learning to a rare-cell clinical task with limited labeled data.

The most consequential single finding of the project was the learning rate mismatch in Phase 2. It is counterintuitive: domain-specific pretraining should help, and it does, but only if the fine-tuning protocol accounts for the architectural state that pretraining leaves the model in. When a single-class YOLO checkpoint is reloaded for two-class fine-tuning, the classification head is randomly initialized while the backbone carries domain-adapted representations. At the default learning rate, the head's random gradients corrupt those representations before they can contribute. P2-C demonstrates this concretely: a domain-relevant starting model at the default learning rate produced recall 0.397, worse than a generic COCO-pretrained model. The recovery to 0.655 recall under reduced learning rate and frozen backbone reveals that the pretraining advantage was real but inaccessible without a careful protocol. This is practically important beyond this specific project: anyone adapting a YOLO model pretrained on one class configuration to a new one will encounter this failure mode silently if they do not reduce the learning rate, and the standard YOLO documentation provides no guidance for this scenario.

The shift to LOPO evaluation in Phase 3 was the most consequential methodological decision of the project, and its justification is precisely quantifiable. Stratified k-fold allows tiles from the same patient to appear in both training and test splits. Within a single patient's slides, staining intensity, scanner calibration, slide preparation technique, and cellular density are internally consistent, while these properties vary substantially between patients. A model evaluated this way can exploit within-patient texture consistency to achieve metrics that do not reflect cross-patient generalization. LOPO eliminates this entirely. The performance figures reported in this thesis are therefore conservative estimates of clinical performance, not optimistic within-patient interpolations. For a tool that will encounter new patients it has never seen, this is the only evaluation that reflects the actual deployment condition.

The DoE matrix versus automated tuner comparison produced a finding that extends well beyond this project's specific setting. The YOLO built-in tuner, after 30 iterations optimizing on a single patient fold (P4), converged on degrees=0.0 and dfl=2.47, both directly contradicted by the matrix evidence. The tuner found a local optimum that worked for P4's specific texture distribution but did not generalize across the heterogeneous eight-patient cohort. The matrix, by evaluating each configuration on all eight patients simultaneously, selected a configuration robust to individual-patient variance. For medical imaging with strong patient-level confounders and a small, heterogeneous cohort, single-fold fitness optimization finds the wrong answer with high confidence. Systematic multi-patient evaluation is not an optional refinement.

## Clinical Relevance

The WHO 2022 minor criterion for SM requires at least 25% of bone marrow mast cells to exhibit atypical morphology. The pipeline's practical clinical value depends on how a recall of 0.866 interacts with that threshold under realistic patient conditions. Because Atypisch and Normal cells are missed at similar rates (R_Atypisch=0.892, R_Normal=0.840), the model's undercount is nearly proportional: both counts are reduced by roughly the same fraction, leaving the Atypisch-to-total ratio approximately preserved. A patient with a true Atypisch fraction of 40% will present a computed fraction near 40% rather than near the diagnostic boundary. The critical zone is the neighborhood around 25%: for patients whose true fraction lies within roughly 5 to 10 percentage points of the threshold, the residual 5.2-percentage-point class imbalance in recall could in principle shift the computed fraction across the boundary. The statistics view in the desktop application makes this boundary proximity explicitly visible, directing the clinician's manual review attention toward exactly the cases where the model's approximation error matters most.

The asymmetric design of the pipeline reflects a deliberate clinical insight maintained throughout the project: recall over precision, at every decision point. The oversampling strategy targeted Normal-class recall specifically. The DoE matrix selected configurations based on per-class recall rather than aggregate mAP. The annotation editor makes false positives, which are visible, easy to remove. This entire stack of decisions rests on the recognition that in a human-in-the-loop review workflow, a false positive is recoverable because it is visible, while a false negative is invisible by definition and requires active search to identify. Designing for high recall and providing tools to correct the resulting false positives is the architecturally appropriate approach for a clinical screening aid, not an autonomous diagnostic system.

## Error Analysis

Three systematic error patterns emerged from the evaluation that are worth examining in detail, because each points to a specific constraint in the current system and to a specific direction for improvement.

The first pattern is the underperformance on the P1 and P5 holdout folds, which score at recall levels of 0.626 and 0.617 against a population mean of 0.866. The explanation for each case is traceable and distinct from any model deficiency. P1 is the only patient in the corpus presenting no Normal cells at all. When P1 is the test patient, the training set contains all other patients' Normal-class data, but the model has never been shown a slide context where Normal cells are entirely absent. The distributional prior at test time is categorically different from everything in training. P5 is the mirror image: three Atypisch cells against eighteen Normal cells makes it the only Normal-dominated case in the dataset, and a model trained on the other seven patients, where Atypisch cells outnumber Normal by a large margin even after oversampling, has simply never encountered a prior distribution that resembles P5's. Both findings converge on the same root cause: the current dataset does not yet cover the full spectrum of clinical presentations, and adding patients with unusual Atypisch-to-Normal ratios is the most direct way to close the gap.

The second pattern involves the DFL loss weight. Increasing DFL from 1.5 to 2.0 consistently degraded Normal-class recall across all freeze and rotation settings tested in the matrix. DFL (Distribution Focal Loss) governs bounding-box localization quality; a higher weight penalizes imprecise box placement more strongly. In a single-cell tile with a uniform background, localization ambiguity is much lower than in natural multi-object scenes, so the additional localization pressure from higher DFL does not improve box quality. Instead, it competes with the classification gradient from the rare Normal class and suppresses the Normal-class learning signal. The consistency of this pattern across matrix cells converts an isolated observation into a generalizable finding: for single-cell morphology detection in clean tiled imaging contexts, the default DFL weight of 1.5 is appropriate and higher values are counterproductive.

The third pattern is the label smoothing no-op. At ls=0.1, a value well within the recommended range for imbalanced small-dataset classification, the Ultralytics training pipeline produced results bit-identical to ls=0.0 across two independent matrix rows. This is unambiguous empirical evidence that label smoothing is inert in this framework configuration. Whether the parameter is silently bypassed in the detection head's loss path for this Ultralytics version, or whether its effect is neutralized by an interaction with the focal loss mechanism in the detection objective, was not conclusively determined. But the empirical result is reproducible, and it matters: a practitioner following the standard recommendation to use label smoothing for imbalanced small-dataset classification in the same framework version would be applying a parameter with no effect while believing it is providing regularization. This finding is worth reporting to the community.

---

# Conclusion

## Summary of Key Findings

This thesis opens a question that no prior published work has directly answered: can a deep learning model perform binary morphological classification of mast cells in bone marrow aspirates in alignment with an established WHO diagnostic threshold, evaluated on independently held-out patient cases? The answer, demonstrated across an eight-patient leave-one-patient-out validation, is yes. The pipeline achieves mean recall of 0.866, mAP50 of 0.864, and per-class recalls of 0.892 for Atypisch and 0.840 for Normal across eight independent patient holdouts, processing clinical datasets of up to 20,000 slide tiles per session within a timeframe practical for clinical review.

Three methodological contributions with implications beyond this specific task were established in the course of development. The first is the learning rate mismatch finding: fine-tuning a YOLO model from a checkpoint with a different class count requires a substantially reduced learning rate and backbone freezing to prevent the randomly initialized classification head from corrupting domain-adapted feature representations. P2-C demonstrates the practical consequences of ignoring this: a domain-specific pretrained model with the wrong learning rate underperforms a generic COCO-pretrained model by 25 recall percentage points. This behavior is not documented in standard YOLO fine-tuning guidance. The second is the tuner-versus-DoE finding: a fitness-optimized automated tuner found a configuration that contradicted the systematic matrix evidence because it optimized on a single patient fold and was blind to cross-patient heterogeneity. For clinical applications with a small, heterogeneous patient cohort, single-fold optimization is an unreliable configuration selection strategy. Systematic multi-patient DoE sweeps are more informative and more robust. The third is the label smoothing no-op: a parameter widely recommended for imbalanced small-dataset classification was empirically confirmed inert across two independent matrix rows in the tested framework version, a reproducible negative finding with practical implications for practitioners using the same tooling.

The bootstrap annotation cycle established in this project represents a transferable contribution for rare-cell annotation tasks in clinical imaging. The model-assisted CVAT-NUCLIO workflow transformed a single-patient manually labeled corpus into an eight-patient labeled dataset with a fraction of the annotation effort that fully manual labeling would have required. Each clinical session with the deployed application continues this cycle: new patient data is processed, corrections are recorded, and the corrected annotations are available for the next training round. The system was designed to improve through use, not to deliver a fixed artifact.

## Limitations and Challenges

The primary constraint on the current results is dataset size. The eight-patient corpus contains 1,103 annotated images with a 14:1 class imbalance, and only four patients contribute substantial Normal-class annotations. The oversampling strategy mitigates this imbalance but cannot resolve it, and the two weakest LOPO folds, P1 and P5, demonstrate precisely what happens when the test patient represents a distribution the training corpus cannot adequately cover. The mean recall of 0.866 should be read as a minimum achievable on this dataset, not as the architecture's ceiling: the same YOLO11n model trained on a corpus of thirty or more patients with balanced Normal-class coverage would almost certainly produce substantially higher values.

A second limitation is the absence of a formal inter-rater agreement assessment. Annotation was performed by a single expert with informal consultation on ambiguous cases. Without a second independent annotator and a measured agreement statistic such as Cohen's kappa, the reproducibility of the ground truth cannot be formally quantified. The reported metrics are therefore conditional on one annotator's definition of atypical versus normal mast cell morphology, which is a common constraint in rare-cell settings where expert capacity is a bottleneck but must be acknowledged explicitly.

A third consideration is institutional scope. All eight patients come from a single institution with a specific scanner model, slide preparation protocol, and staining technique. Performance on data from a different hospital, scanner, or staining laboratory is not guaranteed to match the LOPO estimates. Validation on externally acquired data would be required before the pipeline could be claimed to generalize beyond the USZ context.

## Future Research Directions

The most impactful near-term direction is corpus expansion. The model delivered to the USZ is actively pre-annotating new patient slides, and each corrected session accumulates labeled data for the next training round, particularly for Normal cells and for patient presentations not yet represented in the eight-patient corpus. A second training round on an expanded dataset of twelve or more patients would allow direct comparison with the results reported here and directly test whether the performance gap seen on the P1 and P5 holdout folds closes as the training distribution broadens. This comparison would also validate whether the fine-tuning recipe identified in Phase 3 scales as intended to a larger dataset.

A formal inter-rater reliability study on a representative image subset, involving at least two independent clinical annotators, would strengthen the ground-truth definition and allow the annotation protocol to be specified and reproduced more rigorously. This is particularly relevant for cells near the morphological Atypisch-Normal boundary, where a single annotator's judgment carries full weight in the current protocol and where disagreement between annotators would reveal the ambiguity that the model is being asked to resolve.

On the technical side, the label smoothing no-op finding warrants a targeted investigation into the Ultralytics detection head loss implementation to determine whether the parameter is silently bypassed in the version used. If confirmed as an implementation gap, this is worth reporting to the open-source Ultralytics community. The chunk-based inference architecture in the desktop application could also be extended with a confidence calibration step, converting raw YOLO scores to calibrated probabilities, which would make the threshold more interpretable and allow the statistics view to present uncertainty estimates alongside the Atypisch fraction, giving the clinician a more direct signal about when to trust the model's count and when to review manually.

In the longer term, formal integration of the pipeline into the Cinderella platform remains the logical end state for a tool that has demonstrated clinical utility in standalone testing. The IT governance and API integration work required to achieve this was beyond the thesis scope, but the standalone application provides a concrete operational artifact to reference in any future integration specification. As the annotated corpus grows and model performance stabilizes across a wider range of presentations, the technical risk of integration decreases and the clinical case for it strengthens.
